deutsch-family.title: The complete input family for Deutsch’s problem
deutsch-family.caption: Each row is one hidden device. The algorithm must output \(d=f(0)\oplus f(1)\): it must separate the rows into two classes, not identify the row.

query-superposition.title: One coherent query on a superposition of inputs
query-superposition.caption: \(U_f\) is the two-register oracle, a composite operation. After the query both values of \(f\) appear in the state, but measuring both registers returns one input with its value.

deutsch-circuit.title: Deutsch’s algorithm with one query
deutsch-circuit.caption: Register order is input, then target. The Hadamards prepare \(\ket+\ket-\); the query kicks \((-1)^{f(x)}\) onto the input; the final Hadamard turns the relative sign into the bit \(d\). The target is not measured.

record-circuit.title: A target record prevents cancellation
record-circuit.caption: With target \(\ket0\) and \(f(x)=x\), the query makes the target a copy of the input. After the Hadamard, the minus sign sits on \(\ket{11}\) and cannot cancel the plus sign on \(\ket{10}\); the input outcome is a fair coin.

readout-plane.title: The answer states before the final Hadamard
readout-plane.caption: Constant functions leave the input along \(\ket+\) and balanced functions along \(\ket-\), up to sign. These states are orthogonal, so a measurement in their basis separates them with certainty; the Hadamard rotates that basis onto \(\ket0,\ket1\).

majority-curve.title: Majority voting amplifies a bounded advantage
majority-curve.caption: Probability that the majority of \(R\) independent runs is correct, when each run is correct with probability \(p\). Above \(p=1/2\) the curves steepen as \(R\) grows; at \(p=1/2\) voting cannot help.

access-table.title: Forms of access and what they do not include
access-table.caption: Each form of access is a separate assumption. Possessing one does not provide the others, and each must be implemented and paid for in an end-to-end cost.
rows: Cheap implementation if the sequence is long
A quantum state or oracle without loading cost

dj-circuit.title: The Deutsch–Jozsa circuit on \(n\) input qubits
dj-circuit.caption: The slash marks an \(n\)-qubit register; each \(H\) box is \(n\) Hadamards. The zero outcome has amplitude \(2^{-n}\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}\): magnitude one for a constant function and zero for a balanced one.

deutsch-resources.title: Resources for the Deutsch circuit as drawn
deutsch-resources.caption: Ideal oracle access is assumed. A concrete implementation must add the cost of building the oracle, which the query count deliberately excludes.
rows: Two, plus any workspace inside the oracle
Three Hadamards, and one \(X\) if both qubits start in \(\ket0\)
One: the ideal circuit is exact
Excluded from the query count; charged in a gate count

design-checklist.title: The design process applied to Deutsch’s problem
design-checklist.caption: Each row is a design question that applies to every algorithm in the course. The answers for Deutsch’s problem are developed in the sections before this one.
rows: What output, for which inputs, with what success?
How may the input be consulted?
Coherent oracle \(U_f\), one use per query
How does the property enter amplitudes?
Which branches meet, and what blocks them?
Both inputs meet under \(H\); no target record
Why is it correct on every input?
What does it cost, against which baseline?

technique-map.title: Techniques of the course and where they are used
technique-map.caption: Named algorithms are applications or compositions of techniques. Later chapters reuse the analysis of earlier ones rather than repeating it.
rows: Block encodings, linear combinations of unitaries

clean-contract.title: The clean oracle contract
clean-contract.caption: Slashes mark registers of \(n\), \(m\), and \(w\) qubits. The box may contain many gates and use the workspace freely, but it must return the workspace to \(\ket{0^w}\) on every basis input, with no input-dependent phase.

garbage-circuit.title: Direct reversible translation leaves garbage
garbage-circuit.caption: A Toffoli computes \(g=a\land b\); two CNOTs compute \(t=g\oplus c\). The answer \(t=f(a,b,c)\) is accompanied by the input-dependent garbage bit \(g\).

incrementer.title: Adding one modulo four
incrementer.caption: The high bit \(b_1\) is drawn first. The CNOT adds the carry from the low bit; the \(X\) flips the low bit. The map is \(0\to1\to2\to3\to0\), a permutation, so it acts on superpositions without measurement.

uncompute-circuit.title: Compute, copy, uncompute
uncompute-circuit.caption: Register order \(a,b,c,g,t,y\). The first three gates compute \(g=ab\) and \(t=f\); one CNOT copies \(t\) into the external target \(y\); the last three gates are the first three in reverse order, returning \(g\) and \(t\) to \(\ket0\).

phase-from-clean.title: A phase oracle from a clean computation
phase-from-clean.caption: \(C\) computes \(f(x)\) into the qubit \(t\) together with garbage in the workspace. A \(Z\) on \(t\) multiplies by \((-1)^{f(x)}\); \(C^{-1}\) then clears both \(t\) and the workspace, leaving only the sign on the input.

garbage-test.title: An interference test separates clean from dirty oracles
garbage-test.caption: Input \((\ket{000}+\ket{110})/\sqrt2\); apply the phase oracle, then a CNOT from the first input bit to the second and a Hadamard on the first. Columns show input register and workspace.

cost-table.title: What one gate costs depends on the gate set
cost-table.caption: Typical constructions in the Clifford+\(T\) gate set. Counts are for standard textbook circuits and can be reduced in context, for example when a Toffoli is later uncomputed.
rows: Clifford gates; cheap in most error-corrected schemes

pebble-table.title: Trading time for space in reversible computation
pebble-table.caption: For a chain of \(k\) stages, each computed from the previous one. A pebble is a stored intermediate value. The recursive strategy holds fewer values at once but recomputes some of them.

reflection-circuit.title: Reflection about a prepared state
reflection-circuit.caption: Top: \(R_\psi=A S_0 A^\dagger\) with \(A\ket{0^n}=\ket\psi\); the matrix product is read right to left, the circuit left to right. Bottom: one construction of \(S_0\) on three qubits, up to a global sign: \(X\) on every qubit, a doubly controlled \(Z\), and \(X\) again.

controlled-construction.title: Controlling a known circuit gate by gate
controlled-construction.caption: If \(U=G_2G_1\), then controlled-\(U\) is controlled-\(G_1\) followed by controlled-\(G_2\). On the control-0 branch nothing acts; on the control-1 branch both gates act. The global phase of \(U\) must be fixed first, because it becomes a phase on the control.

output-forms.title: A coherent output is not a table of values
output-forms.caption: A subroutine’s contract should state which output form it delivers. Converting a state into classical data costs repetitions that grow with the amount of data and the precision required.
rows: Nothing directly; it feeds a further circuit

kickback-controlled.title: Phase kickback from an eigenstate
kickback-controlled.caption: With the target in an eigenstate \(\ket u\) of \(V\), controlled-\(V\) leaves the target unchanged and attaches the eigenvalue \(e^{i\phi}\) to the control’s \(\ket1\) branch, where it is a relative phase.

hadamard-test.title: The Hadamard test
hadamard-test.caption: Top: \(\Pr[0]=\tfrac12(1+\operatorname{Re}\bra\psi U\ket\psi)\). Bottom: inserting \(S^\dagger\) on the control gives \(\tfrac12(1+\operatorname{Im}\bra\psi U\ket\psi)\). The controlled-\(U\) is a composite operation and requires controlled access.

hadamard-test-curve.title: A phase becomes a bias
hadamard-test-curve.caption: For an eigenstate with eigenvalue \(e^{i\phi}\), the Hadamard test outputs 0 with probability \((1+\cos\phi)/2\) (solid) and the \(S^\dagger\) variant with probability \((1+\sin\phi)/2\) (dashed). Together they determine \(\phi\).

bit-from-phase.title: A bit oracle from a controlled phase oracle
bit-from-phase.caption: The target \(\ket y\) is moved to the Hadamard basis, used as the control of the phase oracle \(O_f\), and moved back. The control-0 branch receives no sign, which fixes the global phase that an uncontrolled \(O_f\) leaves ambiguous.

hadamard-signs.title: The signs of the two-qubit Hadamard transform
hadamard-signs.caption: Entry \((x,z)\) is the sign of \(\ket z\) in \(H^{\otimes2}\ket x\), namely \((-1)^{x\cdot z}\); every entry also carries the factor \(1/2\). Distinct rows are orthogonal, so a row pattern is mapped back to its label.

bv-circuit.title: The Bernstein–Vazirani circuit for three input bits
bv-circuit.caption: One query to the oracle for \(f_s(x)=s\cdot x\), with the target in \(\ket-\), writes the sign pattern \((-1)^{s\cdot x}\). The final Hadamard layer maps that pattern to \(\ket s\), so the measured bits are \(s_1s_2s_3\) with certainty.

dj-zero-probability.title: The zero outcome outside the promise
dj-zero-probability.caption: For \(n=3\), probability of the all-zero outcome when \(f\) takes the value 1 on \(k\) of the 8 inputs: \((1-k/4)^2\). Only \(k=0,8\) (constant) and \(k=4\) (balanced) give certain answers.

simon-circuit.title: One run of Simon’s algorithm
simon-circuit.caption: Both registers have \(n\) qubits. Measuring the output collapses the input onto a pair \(\{x_0,x_0\oplus s\}\); the Hadamard layer turns the unknown \(x_0\) into a phase and returns a random \(z\) with \(s\cdot z=0\). The output measurement may be omitted without changing the statistics of \(z\).

simon-example.title: Simon’s algorithm for n = 3 and s = 110
simon-example.caption: Collision pairs \(\{x,x\oplus s\}\), the strings \(z\) the circuit can return, and how two independent samples determine \(s\) by linear algebra modulo two.
rows: each pair shares one value of \(f\)

phase-gates.title: A phase from a computed integer
phase-gates.caption: \(C\) computes a three-bit value \(v=4v_2+2v_1+v_0\) from \(x\). Phase gates \(Z\), \(S\), \(T\) on the bits multiply by \(e^{2\pi iv/8}\); \(C^{-1}\) then clears the register so that only the phase remains on \(\ket x\).

fourier-kickback.title: Phase kickback from modular addition
fourier-kickback.caption: The register holding \(\ket\chi=M^{-1/2}\sum_ye^{-2\pi iy/M}\ket y\) is an eigenstate of adding \(v\) modulo \(M\), with eigenvalue \(e^{2\pi iv/M}\). A clean addition of a computed \(v(x)\) therefore kicks the phase back onto \(\ket x\) and leaves \(\ket\chi\) unchanged for reuse.

precision-table.title: Phase precision as a resource
precision-table.caption: Errors are measured in operator norm, the largest change to any normalized state. Because unitaries preserve length, errors of composed operations add.

roots-of-unity.title: The eighth roots of unity
roots-of-unity.caption: The powers of \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/8}\) are eight equally spaced unit arrows. Their sum is zero, and so is the sum of \(\omega^{kx}\) over \(x\) for any \(k\) not divisible by 8: the arrows are evenly spread, possibly winding several times around the circle.

periodic-fourier.title: A period-2 pattern becomes two frequencies
periodic-fourier.caption: Probabilities before and after \(F_8\) for the state \(\tfrac12(\ket0+\ket2+\ket4+\ket6)\). Four positions spaced by 2 become two frequencies spaced by \(8/2=4\). Shifting the input pattern by one changes only phases of the output, not these probabilities.

qft-three.title: The quantum Fourier transform on three qubits
qft-three.caption: Inputs \(x_2x_1x_0\), high bit on top. Each wire receives a Hadamard and controlled phase gates \(P(\pi/2)\), \(P(\pi/4)\) from lower bits, building the factors of the product representation in reverse order; the final swap restores the order. Output \(y_2y_1y_0\).

aqft-table.title: Exact and approximate Fourier transforms
aqft-table.caption: Dropping controlled rotations with angle below \(2\pi/2^b\) changes the transform by less than \(2\pi n/2^b\) in operator norm. Counts are for \(n\) qubits; each kept rotation must still be synthesized in a fault-tolerant gate set.

qpe-circuit.title: Phase estimation with three control qubits
qpe-circuit.caption: The target holds an eigenstate \(\ket u\) of \(U\) with eigenvalue \(e^{2\pi i\phi}\). Control \(j\) applies \(U^{2^j}\) and receives the phase \(e^{2\pi i2^j\phi}\); the inverse Fourier transform \(F^\dagger\) (a composite operation) maps the resulting phase ramp to the digits of \(\phi\).

qpe-bits.title: Phase estimation for φ = 3/8 = 0.011 in binary
qpe-bits.caption: Each control qubit carries the phase \(2^j\phi\) modulo one, which depends only on the digits of \(\phi\) after position \(j\). The highest control holds the last digit as a sign; the inverse Fourier transform removes the known contributions and reads every digit exactly.

qpe-distribution.title: Phase estimation for a phase between grid points
qpe-distribution.caption: Outcome probabilities for \(M=8\) and \(\phi=0.3\), so \(M\phi=2.4\). The two nearest grid points 2 and 3 carry probability about 0.84; the distribution falls off roughly as the inverse square of the distance from \(M\phi\).

qpe-mixture.title: Phase estimation on a superposition of eigenstates
qpe-mixture.caption: For \(\ket\psi=\sum_sc_s\ket{u_s}\), phase estimation returns an estimate of one eigenphase \(\phi_s\), chosen with probability \(|c_s|^2\), and leaves the target close to \(\ket{u_s}\). It samples eigenvalues; it does not list them.

orbit-table.title: The orbit of 1 under multiplication by 7 modulo 15
orbit-table.caption: \(U_7\) cycles \(1\to7\to4\to13\to1\), so the order is \(r=4\). Classically, finding \(r\) by following the orbit can take a number of steps comparable to \(L\).

order-finding-circuit.title: Order finding by phase estimation
order-finding-circuit.caption: The control register has \(m\approx2n\) qubits; the target has \(n\) qubits and starts in \(\ket1\), an equal superposition of the eigenstates \(\ket{u_s}\). The modular exponentiation box, \(\ket k\ket y\mapsto\ket k\ket{a^ky\bmod L}\), is the controlled powers and contains most of the gates.

continued-fraction.title: Recovering r = 6 from the outcome 85/512
continued-fraction.caption: Euclid’s algorithm gives \(85/512=[0;6,42,2]\). The last convergent with denominator below \(L=21\) is \(1/6\), so the candidate order is 6, confirmed by \(2^6\equiv1\pmod{21}\).

factoring-flow.title: Shor’s reduction from factoring to order finding
factoring-flow.caption: Only the order-finding step is quantum. For odd \(L\) with at least two distinct prime factors, each random \(a\) succeeds with probability at least 1/2; failures lead back to a new random choice.
factoring-flow.summary: Flowchart. Pick a random a. If gcd(a, L) > 1, a factor is found. Otherwise run quantum order finding to get r. If r is even and a^(r/2) is not −1 mod L, gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, L) are factors; if not, pick a new a. Example L = 21, a = 2: gcd is 1, r = 6, 2^3 = 8 ≢ −1, and gcd(7, 21) = 7, gcd(9, 21) = 3.

shor-resources.title: Where the cost of Shor’s algorithm goes
shor-resources.caption: Asymptotic counts for an \(n\)-bit modulus with schoolbook arithmetic. Concrete estimates for cryptographic sizes also depend on the error-correction scheme, physical error rates, and arithmetic optimizations.

hsp-table.title: Hidden subgroup problems
hsp-table.caption: The same pattern, superposition, evaluation, coset collapse, Fourier transform, sampling, solves the problem efficiently for abelian groups. For the nonabelian cases shown, no efficient quantum algorithm is known.

good-bad-plane.title: Amplification in the good–bad plane
good-bad-plane.caption: The prepared state \(\ket\psi\) lies at angle \(\theta\) above the bad axis, with \(\sin^2\theta=p\). The predicate reflection \(S_G\) sends it to angle \(-\theta\); the reflection about \(\ket\psi\) then sends it to \(3\theta\). Each iteration rotates by \(2\theta\) toward \(\ket G\). Drawn for \(\theta=20^\circ\).

iteration-circuit.title: One amplification iteration
iteration-circuit.caption: \(S_G\) is the clean phase oracle for the predicate; \(A^\dagger\), the zero-state reflection \(S_0\), and \(A\) together reflect about \(\ket\psi=A\ket{0^n}\). Each box can contain many gates; \(A\) is often the most expensive part.

success-oscillation.title: Success probability oscillates with the number of iterations
success-oscillation.caption: For \(p=0.01\), the success probability after \(k\) iterations is \(\sin^2((2k+1)\theta)\) with \(\theta=\arcsin0.1\). It peaks near \(k=7\), returns almost to zero near \(k=15\), and keeps oscillating. More iterations are not always better.

iteration-table.title: Optimal iteration counts
iteration-table.caption: \(k=\operatorname{round}(\pi/(4\theta)-1/2)\) and the resulting success probability, compared with the expected number of independent classical tries, \(1/p\), before the first success. For \(p=1/2\) no iteration helps.

exact-amplification.title: Exact amplification by lowering the angle
exact-amplification.caption: With \(p\) known, choose \(k=\lceil\pi/(4\theta)-1/2\rceil\) and \(\theta'=\pi/(4k+2)\le\theta\). A flag qubit with probability \(p'/p\) of being 1 reduces the success probability to \(p'=\sin^2\theta'\), and \(k\) iterations on the joint preparation then succeed with certainty.

fixed-point-curve.title: Ordinary versus fixed-point amplification
fixed-point-curve.caption: Success probability after one step as a function of the initial success probability \(p\). An ordinary iteration (\(\sin^2(3\theta)\)) is excellent near \(p=1/4\) but overshoots for larger \(p\). One \(\pi/3\) fixed-point step (\(1-(1-p)^3\)) never decreases success. Both use three calls to \(A\) or \(A^\dagger\).

ae-eigen.title: The Grover iterate as a rotation with complex eigenvectors
ae-eigen.caption: In the good–bad plane, \(Q\) rotates by \(2\theta\). Its eigenvectors \(\ket{v_\pm}=(\ket G\pm i\ket B)/\sqrt2\) have eigenphases \(\pm2\theta\), and \(\ket\psi\) has equal weight on both, so phase estimation returns \(\theta/\pi\) or \(1-\theta/\pi\), each with probability 1/2.

ae-circuit.title: Amplitude estimation
ae-circuit.caption: Phase estimation applied to the Grover iterate \(Q\), starting from \(A\ket{0^n}\). The controlled powers of \(Q\) cost \(M-1\) controlled iterations for \(M=2^m\); each contains \(A\), \(A^\dagger\), and an oracle call. The outcome \(j\) gives \(\tilde p=\sin^2(\pi j/M)\).

ae-cost.title: Sampling versus amplitude estimation
ae-cost.caption: Calls to \(A\) needed to estimate \(p\approx0.3\) to additive precision \(\epsilon\) with constant confidence. Sampling uses many short independent runs; amplitude estimation uses one long coherent circuit with controlled access to \(A\) and \(A^\dagger\).

mean-estimation.title: Encoding a mean as a success probability
mean-estimation.caption: \(P\) prepares \(\sum_x\sqrt{q(x)}\ket x\). The rotation, controlled on a clean computation of \(v(x)\in[0,1]\), puts amplitude \(\sqrt{v(x)}\) on the flag value 1, so the flag is 1 with probability \(\mathbb E[v]\). This whole circuit is the \(A\) handed to amplitude estimation.

min-finding.title: Minimum finding as amplification in a classical loop
min-finding.caption: Each round uses exponential search with a comparator predicate. The expected total number of queries is O(√N); the comparator and the oracle for T are charged per query.
min-finding.summary: A loop. Start with a random candidate y. While the query budget lasts, run a quantum threshold search for some x with T(x) < T(y); if it returns a better x, set y to x, and repeat. When the budget is exhausted, output y.

notes.text: expected total queries \(O(\sqrt N)\); comparator and \(T\)-oracle charged per query

search-limits.title: What amplification can and cannot do
search-limits.caption: Query counts in the black-box model. The \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\) bound holds for every quantum algorithm that accesses the input only through the oracle; larger speedups need structure.

classical-walk.title: A random walk on a four-cycle
classical-walk.caption: Each step moves to one of the two neighbours with probability 1/2. Probabilities of routes multiply along a route and add across routes; nothing can cancel. After \(t\) steps on the line, the spread is about \(\sqrt t\).

notes.text: each vertex also steps the other way with probability 1/2 (arrows show one direction)

coined-step.title: One step of a coined walk on a cycle
coined-step.caption: The coin qubit is rotated by \(H\); then the position register is decremented if the coin is 0 (open control) and incremented if it is 1 (filled control), modulo \(N\). Each shift box is reversible arithmetic built as in the Coherent Computation chapter.

walk-spread.title: Quantum and classical walks after 60 steps
walk-spread.caption: Position distributions on the line after \(T=60\) steps (even positions only; odd positions have probability zero). The Hadamard walk (bars) spreads to about \(\pm T/\sqrt2\) with standard deviation about \(0.54T\approx32\); the classical walk (curve) has standard deviation \(\sqrt T\approx7.7\).

two-vertex-walk.title: Coherent oscillation versus classical mixing
two-vertex-walk.caption: Probability of finding the walker at the second vertex. The quantum walk with \(H=\gamma X\) oscillates as \(\sin^2(\gamma t)\) and never settles; the classical continuous random walk approaches 1/2 monotonically.

spectral-evolution.title: Evolving through eigenvectors
spectral-evolution.caption: For \(H=\gamma X\), expand \(\ket0\) in eigenvectors, give each its phase \(e^{-i\lambda t}\), and recombine. Motion comes from the difference between the two phases.

cycle-spectrum.title: Eigenvalues of a cycle are cosines
cycle-spectrum.caption: The adjacency matrix of a cycle of \(N=12\) vertices has Fourier modes as eigenvectors, with eigenvalues \(2\cos(2\pi k/N)\) (bars). The curve shows the continuous dispersion relation; its slope sets the speed of a wave packet.

szegedy-step.title: One step of Szegedy’s walk
szegedy-step.caption: \(V\ket x\ket0=\ket x\sum_y\sqrt{P_{xy}}\ket y\). The first three boxes reflect about the span of the states \(\ket{\psi_x}\) (\(R_A\)); swapping the registers and repeating gives \(R_B\). Each \(V\) needs coherent access to the neighbours of a vertex.

gap-curve.title: A spectral gap becomes a larger phase gap
gap-curve.caption: For a classical gap \(\delta\), the walk’s phase gap is \(2\arccos(1-\delta)\) (solid), at least \(2\sqrt\delta\) (dashed). For small \(\delta\) the phase gap is much larger than \(\delta\) itself (dotted), which is why phase estimation can detect it in order \(1/\sqrt\delta\) steps.

walk-search-table.title: Classical and quantum walk search
walk-search-table.caption: Costs in walk steps and checks, with setup omitted. \(\varepsilon\) is the marked fraction and \(\delta\) the spectral gap. The quantum framework square-roots both factors.

element-distinctness.title: Element distinctness on the Johnson graph
element-distinctness.caption: Vertices are \(r\)-subsets with their stored values. Choosing \(r=N^{2/3}\) balances setup against search and gives \(O(N^{2/3})\) queries, which is optimal. The algorithm stores \(r\) values in coherent memory.
rows: query every element of the first subset
swap one element, reuse the rest
subset must contain both colliding indices

walk-results.title: What quantum walks achieve
walk-results.caption: Query complexities with coherent neighbour access. Time complexity adds the cost of implementing that access and any coherent data structures.

nonunitary-stretch.title: A non-unitary matrix changes lengths unevenly
nonunitary-stretch.caption: \(A=\mathrm{diag}(1,\tfrac12)\) leaves \(\ket0\) unchanged, halves \(\ket1\), and maps \(\ket+\) to a vector of length \(\sqrt{5/8}\) pointing closer to \(\ket0\). No unitary, which preserves every length, can do this. (Vectors are drawn at unit length; the legend gives the true lengths.)

block-encoding-circuit.title: A block encoding with one ancilla
block-encoding-circuit.caption: \(U\) acts on the ancilla and the system. With the ancilla starting in \(\ket0\), the ancilla-0 branch of the output is \(A\ket\psi/\alpha\) and the ancilla-1 branch carries the remaining length. Measuring the ancilla and keeping outcome 0 applies \(A\) up to normalization.

postselection-table.title: Postselection for A = diag(1, 1/2)
postselection-table.caption: Success probability \(\|A\psi\|^2/\alpha^2\) (here \(\alpha=1\)) and the normalized output on success. The success probability depends on the input; it is the price of applying a non-unitary map.

lcu-circuit.title: Linear combination of unitaries
lcu-circuit.caption: PREPARE loads the weights \(\sqrt{a_j/\alpha}\) into the ancilla register; SELECT applies \(U_j\) on the branch \(\ket j\); un-preparing and keeping ancilla outcome 0 leaves \(\sum_ja_jU_j\ket\psi/\alpha\). SELECT is a multiplexed controlled operation and is usually the most expensive part.

lcu-example.title: A block encoding of (I + X)/2
lcu-example.caption: PREPARE is a Hadamard on the ancilla; SELECT is a CNOT. On system input \(\ket0\), ancilla outcome 0 occurs with probability 1/2 and leaves \(\ket+\). A random choice between \(I\) and \(X\) would instead give a mixture of \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\).

pauli-lcu.title: An LCU block encoding of a two-qubit Hamiltonian
pauli-lcu.caption: For \(H=0.5\,Z\otimes Z-0.3\,X\otimes I\), the 1-norm is \(\lambda=0.8\). The sign of the second coefficient is absorbed into its unitary. The circuit encodes \(H/0.8\).

product-encoding.title: Multiplying encoded matrices
product-encoding.caption: \(U_B\) encodes \(B/\beta\) with its own ancillas and \(U_A\) encodes \(A/\alpha\) with others. Keeping both ancilla registers at 0 applies \(AB/(\alpha\beta)\). Reusing one ancilla register for both would let failure amplitude return to the selected block.

error-table.title: How block-encoding errors combine
error-table.caption: Errors are operator-norm distances between the implemented and intended blocks. Because blocks have norm at most one, errors add to first order. An error in the block \(A/\alpha\) corresponds to an error \(\alpha\) times larger in \(A\).

oaa-circuit.title: Oblivious amplitude amplification
oaa-circuit.caption: If \(W\) block-encodes \(\tfrac12V\) with \(V\) unitary, one round, \(W\), the ancilla reflection \(R\), \(W^\dagger\), \(R\), \(W\), yields \(\ket0V\ket\psi\) exactly for every input. \(R\) acts only on the ancillas, so no knowledge of \(\ket\psi\) is needed.

access-models.title: How a matrix can be given
access-models.caption: The subnormalization and cost of a block encoding depend on the access model. Query counts of later algorithms are multiplied by the cost of one block encoding.

dequantization-table.title: Speedups under compatible access
dequantization-table.caption: When quantum algorithms assume data structures that support efficient state preparation, classical algorithms given the matching sampling access can sometimes match them up to polynomial factors.

chebyshev.title: Responses of repeated signal calls
chebyshev.caption: The top-left entry of \(W(x)^d\) is the Chebyshev polynomial \(T_d(x)=\cos(d\arccos x)\). Each is bounded by 1 on \([-1,1]\) and oscillates more as \(d\) grows. Note \(T_2(x)=2x^2-1\), not \(x^2\).

qsp-circuit.title: A quantum signal processing sequence
qsp-circuit.caption: Signal calls \(W(x)\) alternate with \(Z\)-rotations by the phase factors \(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d\). The top-left entry of the product is a polynomial \(P(x)\) of degree at most \(d\); the phases select which polynomial.

parity-table.title: Constraints on achievable responses
parity-table.caption: With \(d\) signal calls the response is a polynomial of degree at most \(d\) with the parity of \(d\), bounded by 1 on \([-1,1]\). Functions without these properties are split, scaled, or restricted.
rows: smooth across a gap of width \(\Delta\)
scale to \(x\), or restrict the interval

eigen-transform.title: Functions of a Hermitian matrix
eigen-transform.caption: A function acts on each eigenvalue separately, \(f(H)=\sum_jf(\lambda_j)\ket{v_j}\bra{v_j}\), and so on every component of a superposition at once, without measuring which eigenvector is present.

qubitization-circuit.title: The qubitized walk
qubitization-circuit.caption: \(U\) is a Hermitian block encoding of \(H/\alpha\); \(R\) reflects about the ancillas being zero. For each eigenvalue \(\lambda_j\), \(W=RU\) rotates within its own plane by \(\theta_j=\arccos(\lambda_j/\alpha)\), so phase rotations on the ancilla between steps implement signal processing on every eigenvalue at once.

svd-picture.title: Singular value transformation
svd-picture.caption: QSVT replaces each singular value \(\sigma_j\) of \(A/\alpha\) by \(P(\sigma_j/\alpha)\). Odd polynomials map input directions to output directions; even polynomials map input directions to themselves.

filter-curve.title: A polynomial filter
filter-curve.caption: A degree-24 even polynomial (solid) approximating a smoothed filter that keeps eigenvalues with \(|x|<0.3\) and removes those with \(|x|>0.5\) (the gap between is shaded by the transition). The polynomial stays within \([-1,1]\) everywhere, as any achievable response must.

inverse-curve.title: A bounded approximation to the inverse
inverse-curve.caption: For \(\kappa=5\), the target \(0.9/(\kappa x)\) (dashed) on \(|x|\ge1/\kappa\), and an odd degree-41 polynomial (solid) that follows it there and stays bounded near zero, where no singular values lie. The success amplitude is at least about \(1/\kappa\).

simulation-degree.title: Why simulation degree is about αt
simulation-degree.caption: \(\log_{10}|J_k(\tau)|\) for \(\tau=\alpha t=20\). The Jacobi–Anger coefficients of \(e^{-i\tau x}\) stay of moderate size up to \(k\approx\tau\) and then fall off faster than exponentially, so truncating at \(k\approx\tau+O(\log(1/\epsilon))\) costs little extra degree for high precision.

simulation-problem.title: The Hamiltonian simulation problem
simulation-problem.caption: Inputs, output, and the resources a simulation method is charged for. The time dependence is at least linear in general (no fast-forwarding).
rows: term exponentials, or a block encoding of \(H/\lambda\)

trotter-circuit.title: First-order product formula for X + Z
trotter-circuit.caption: One step applies \(e^{-i\delta X}\) and then \(e^{-i\delta Z}\) with \(\delta=t/r\); the step is repeated \(r\) times. As a matrix product, the step is \(e^{-i\delta Z}e^{-i\delta X}\) read right to left.

trotter-error.title: First-order Trotter error: bound and reality
trotter-error.caption: Operator-norm error of \((e^{-iX/r}e^{-iZ/r})^r\) against \(e^{-i(X+Z)}\) (solid), and the commutator bound \(t^2\|[X,Z]\|/(2r)=1/r\) (dashed), on logarithmic axes. Both fall as \(1/r\); the bound is about 40% above the actual error.

trotter-orders.title: First- and second-order formulas
trotter-orders.caption: Error for \(e^{-i(X+Z)}\) with \(r\) steps of the first-order formula (falls as \(1/r\)) and of the symmetric second-order formula (falls as \(1/r^2\)), on logarithmic axes. At \(r=10\) the errors are about 0.07 and 0.003.

pauli-exponential.title: Exponential of a Pauli string
pauli-exponential.caption: \(e^{-i\theta X_1Z_2Z_3}\): a Hadamard turns \(X_1\) into \(Z_1\); a CNOT ladder computes the parity of the three bits into the last qubit; \(R_z(2\theta)=e^{-i\theta Z}\) applies the phase; the ladder and basis change are undone.

method-table.title: Three families of simulation methods
method-table.caption: Costs for \(H=\sum_jh_jP_j\) with \(L\) terms and 1-norm \(\lambda\), up to constants and logarithmic factors. Block-encoding calls each cost a PREPARE and SELECT over all terms.

error-budget.title: An error budget for a simulation
error-budget.caption: Each source must be estimated separately; tightening one beyond the others wastes resources.

adiabatic-spectrum.title: Energies along an adiabatic path
adiabatic-spectrum.caption: Eigenvalues \(\pm\sqrt{(1-s)^2+s^2}\) of \(H(s)=-(1-s)X-sZ\). The gap is smallest at \(s=1/2\), where it equals \(\sqrt2\). The ground state rotates from \(\ket+\) at \(s=0\) to \(\ket0\) at \(s=1\).

adiabatic-fidelity.title: Slow enough evolution follows the ground state
adiabatic-fidelity.caption: Probability of ending in \(\ket0\) after evolving under \(H(s)\) with \(s=t/T\), starting from \(\ket+\), as a function of total time \(T\) (numerical simulation). It rises from the sudden value 1/2 to nearly 1 once \(T\) is several times \(1/g_{\min}^2\).

adiabatic-limits.title: What adiabatic optimization achieves
adiabatic-limits.caption: Runtimes are governed by the minimum gap along the path. Small worked examples and proofs for search do not establish efficiency for hard optimization problems.

ansatz-circuit.title: A one-parameter entangled ansatz
ansatz-circuit.caption: \(R_y(\theta)=e^{-i\theta Y/2}\) followed by a CNOT prepares \(\cos\tfrac\theta2\ket{00}+\sin\tfrac\theta2\ket{11}\). Measure directly to estimate \(\langle ZZ\rangle\), or after \(H\) on both qubits to estimate \(\langle XX\rangle\).

vqe-landscape.title: The energy landscape of the example
vqe-landscape.caption: \(E(\theta)=\langle ZZ\rangle\cdot(-1)+\langle XX\rangle\cdot(-1)=-1-\sin\theta\) for \(H=-Z\otimes Z-X\otimes X\). The minimum \(-2\) at \(\theta=\pi/2\) is the exact ground energy, reached because the family contains the Bell state.

shot-table.title: Shots needed to estimate an energy
shot-table.caption: With optimal shot allocation \(R_j\propto|h_j|\sigma_j\), the variance is at most \(\lambda^2/R\), so precision \(\epsilon\) needs about \(\lambda^2/\epsilon^2\) shots per energy evaluation. An optimization needs many evaluations.

parameter-shift.title: Exact gradients from shifted circuits
parameter-shift.caption: For a single Pauli rotation, \(E(\theta)\) is a sinusoid, and \(\tfrac12[E(\theta+\pi/2)-E(\theta-\pi/2)]\) equals the derivative exactly. In the example, \(E=-1-\sin\theta\) (solid) and \(dE/d\theta=-\cos\theta\) (dashed).

noise-table.title: Two kinds of noise in variational methods
noise-table.caption: Shot noise is statistical and averages away with more measurements; hardware noise biases the estimate and does not.

barren-plateau.title: Barren plateaus: causes and responses
barren-plateau.caption: A barren plateau makes gradients exponentially small in the number of qubits, so estimating them needs exponentially many shots. Avoiding one is necessary for training but does not guarantee success.
rows: state approaches the maximally mixed state

vqe-loop.title: The variational loop
vqe-loop.caption: The quantum computer prepares trial states and measures Pauli groups; the classical computer estimates \(E(\theta)\) and its gradient and chooses new parameters. The loop repeats until improvements fall below their statistical uncertainty.
vqe-loop.summary: A loop across two machines. On the quantum computer: prepare U(θ)|0ⁿ⟩, then measure grouped Pauli strings. The bit strings go to the classical computer, which estimates E(θ) and its gradient and updates θ; the new θ returns to the quantum computer. The loop stops when improvements fall below their statistical uncertainty.

notes.text: repeat until improvements fall below their statistical uncertainty

qaoa-landscape.title: Depth-1 QAOA on a single edge
qaoa-landscape.caption: Expected cut \(F(\gamma,\beta)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\sin(4\beta)\sin\gamma\). Varying \(\beta\) at \(\gamma=\pi/2\) (solid) and varying \(\gamma\) at \(\beta=\pi/8\) (dashed); both reach 1 at \(\gamma=\pi/2\), \(\beta=\pi/8\). Other parameters can also minimize the cut.

evidence-table.title: What kind of evidence supports a claim
evidence-table.caption: Variational algorithms are heuristics. Different claims need different kinds of evidence; small successful instances support only the weakest.
rows: The ansatz contains a good state
exact classical optimization over the ansatz on small instances
success rates across random initializations and instances
results across a range of sizes, with fitted scaling
beats the best classical methods at matched quality, total cost counted
a proof, such as an approximation ratio

feedforward-circuit.title: Measurement with feedforward
feedforward-circuit.caption: The first qubit of \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{00}+\ket{11})\) is measured; the outcome, carried on the double line, controls an \(X\) on the second qubit. Both branches end with the second qubit in \(\ket0\): a random outcome has been turned into a deterministic state.

deferred-measurement.title: Deferring a measurement
deferred-measurement.caption: Top: measure, then apply \(V\) if the outcome is 1. Bottom: apply controlled-\(V\) coherently and measure the control at the end. The joint distribution of all final outcomes is the same; the resources are not.

correction-circuit.title: A measurement-dependent Pauli correction
correction-circuit.caption: The Hadamard-test circuit with controlled-\(e^{i\theta X}\). Outcome 0 applies \(e^{i\theta X/2}\); outcome 1 applies \(e^{i\theta X/2}X\), which the classically controlled \(X\) corrects. The data ends in \(e^{i\theta X/2}\ket\psi\) for every input, and the outcome reveals nothing about \(\ket\psi\).

iterative-pe-circuit.title: One stage of iterative phase estimation
iterative-pe-circuit.caption: At stage \(k\), the single control qubit applies \(U^{2^{k-1}}\), receives a phase-gate correction \(P(-\omega_k)\) computed from the bits already measured, and is read in the Hadamard basis to give \(b_k\). It is then reset for the next stage.

iterative-table.title: Iterative phase estimation for φ = 3/8 = 0.011 in binary
iterative-table.caption: Bits are acquired from last to first. Each correction subtracts the contribution of the bits already known, leaving a phase of 0 or \(\pi\) that a Hadamard reads exactly.

heisenberg-curve.title: Two scalings of phase estimation
heisenberg-curve.caption: Error in an estimated phase against total uses \(N\) of \(U\), on logarithmic axes (constants omitted). Repeating independent single-use experiments gives the standard quantum limit \(1/\sqrt N\); coherent powers with adaptive or Fourier processing reach the Heisenberg limit \(1/N\).

one-bit-teleport.title: Applying a gate by one-bit teleportation
one-bit-teleport.caption: Controlled-\(Z\) entangles the input with an auxiliary \(\ket+\). Measuring the input in the basis \(\ket{\pm_\alpha}\) (a phase gate \(P(-\alpha)\), a Hadamard, and a computational-basis measurement) leaves \(X^mHP(-\alpha)\ket\psi\) on the auxiliary qubit; the classically controlled \(X\) removes the byproduct.

cluster-chain.title: Measurement-based computation on a chain
cluster-chain.caption: Qubits in \(\ket+\) entangled by controlled-\(Z\) gates form a cluster chain. Measuring qubit 1 at angle \(\alpha_1\) and qubit 2 at angle \(\alpha_2\) (each a basis change followed by measurement) applies \(HP(-\alpha_2)HP(-\alpha_1)\) to the input, up to Pauli byproducts tracked in the Pauli frame. The second angle depends on the first outcome.

magic-injection.title: Injecting a T gate from a magic state
magic-injection.caption: A CNOT from the data to the magic state \(\ket A=T\ket+\), a measurement of the magic qubit, and a classically controlled \(S\) apply \(T\) to the data. Only Clifford operations act; the non-Clifford resource is the state \(\ket A\), prepared and distilled separately.
